docs.title: TAK-XVoice
docs.text:
TAK-XVoice (XV) is an ATAK voice plugin focused on operational use cases that existing options don't cover well: clean Bluetooth audio routing, predictable auto-reconnect, curated external PTT hardware, and a unified Mumble + multicast voice experience.

Status & Intended Use

TAK-XVoice is provided for non-mission-critical use only. It is distributed under the Apache License 2.0 with no warranty of any kind. Do not rely on this plugin as the sole means of communication for any life-safety, public-safety, military, or other mission-critical application. Operators assume all risk associated with its use.

docs.title: Where to Start
docs.text:
• Quick Start — Install the plugin, connect to your TAK/Mumble server, and make your first PTT transmission.
  • User Setup — Configure Bluetooth audio routing, auto-start missions, talk-permit tones, emergency buttons, and channel sharing.
  • Server & Channels — Mumble host/port requirements (same hostname as your TAK server on standard port 64738), TLS cert authentication, and channel synchronization with TAK Server groups.
  • Supported Hardware — Curated Bluetooth speaker-mics, BLE PTT pucks, and ruggedized handset keys.
  • Dependencies — ATAK versions, Android permissions, server prerequisites, and source build setup.

docs.title: What Makes TAK-XVoice Different
docs.text:
• Phone stays a phone: Your Bluetooth speaker-mic is treated as XV-exclusive comms gear. HFP/SCO only engages while the mic is actually open (PTT-down or hot-mic), so music, navigation prompts, and ATAK alerts keep flowing on their normal audio paths.
  • Predictable auto-reconnect: Remembers your last-used mission and auto-reconnects on plugin start, with an optional configurable startup mission for fleet-managed deployments.
  • Curated PTT hardware: Per-MAC button registration with vetted defaults for supported Bluetooth speaker-mics (AINA APTT V2/V1, Pryme BT-PTT-Z, experimental Inrico BT02) and ruggedized handset keys (Samsung Active Key, including background and locked-screen PTT via Samsung's native key mapping).
  • LMR-familiar UX: Configurable Talk Permit Tones (ASTRO 25, Nextel, DMR, MOTOTRBO, or None), LMR-style emergency button wired into ATAK's Alert Tool, and direct calling.
  • Mumble + multicast under one UX: Mumble authenticates with your device's ATAK enrollment certificate; optional alpha mesh-voice failover provides deterministic multicast voice (xv-mcast-v1) when the server is unreachable.

docs.title: Hardware Philosophy
docs.text: The goal is not to claim support for every Bluetooth PTT device on the market. Each device listed under Supported Hardware is deliberately curated — sourced, integrated, and validated against real event traffic — so operators can trust that what's listed actually works under load. Devices that fail to meet that bar are retired with a public rationale.

docs.title: Privacy Policy
docs.text:
TAK-XVoice ("XV", "the plugin") is an open-source voice plugin for the Android Team Awareness Kit (ATAK), distributed under the Apache License 2.0. This policy explains what the plugin does and does not do with your data. A standalone copy lives at privacy.html.

Last updated: 13 November 2026

docs.title: The short version
docs.text: XV does not collect, store, or transmit personal information to its developers. It has no analytics, no advertising, and no crash-reporting services. To carry your voice, XV connects to the voice server you configure and sends that server -- and the other people on your channel -- your live voice audio and the identity you connect under (your ATAK callsign plus a device-derived identifier). Nothing is ever sent to the plugin's developers.

docs.title: What the plugin accesses, and why
docs.text:
• Microphone / audio. When you press to talk (or a call is active), XV captures audio and transmits it in real time to the voice server you have configured in ATAK. This audio is not recorded to storage by the plugin and is not sent to the plugin's developers.

  • Bluetooth. Used only to connect to and read button presses from the Bluetooth push-to-talk hardware you pair. No Bluetooth data leaves your device.

  • Phone / call state. Used only to detect whether a cellular call is in progress (so push-to-talk behaves correctly) and to register XV's voice session with Android's self-managed calling framework, which lets the plugin manage its own audio routing while you transmit. The plugin does not read your phone number, call log, or contacts, and does not place telephone calls.

  • Network state. Read only to react to Wi-Fi / cellular / offline transitions. The plugin does not change your network settings.

  • Notifications, full-screen intent, wake lock, battery-optimization exemption. Used to show call and status notifications and to keep a voice session alive while the screen is off. No data is collected.

docs.title: Location
docs.text: XV does not request or use location. Bluetooth scanning is declared with the "never for location" flag.

docs.title: Data sharing
docs.text:
The plugin shares no data with its developers. It has no developer-side servers and receives nothing from you.

To use XV you connect to a voice (Mumble/TAK) server that you configure, operated by you or your organization. So that server and the other participants on your channel can carry your voice and show who is speaking, XV sends them:

  • your voice audio, in real time -- never recorded or stored by XV;

  • your connection identity -- your ATAK callsign combined with a device-derived identifier (a one-way hash of your device's ATAK ID, which gives you two voice "slots" and lets other XV users match your voice to your map presence). If you turn on the optional legacy-compatibility mode, your raw ATAK device ID is also sent for the same mapping.

This information goes only to the server you configure and the peers on it -- never to the plugin's developers. How that server and those peers handle it is governed by their own policies; a server operator or another participant could record what they receive, which is outside XV's control.

docs.title: Data retention and deletion
docs.text: The plugin stores only your local settings (such as device pairings and preferences) on your own device. Uninstalling the plugin removes them. There is no developer-side account or storage, so there is nothing for the developers to retain or delete.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Voice traffic to a Mumble server is encrypted in transit with TLS. The optional mesh-voice feature additionally encrypts each audio frame with authenticated encryption (ChaCha20-Poly1305).

docs.title: Children
docs.text: XV is a tool for adult communications volunteers and is not directed at children.

docs.title: Changes
docs.text: This policy may be updated as the plugin evolves. Material changes will be reflected here with a new "last updated" date.

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: Questions about this policy: support@texas-tak.com. Source and issue tracker: github.com/TX-TAK/TAK-XVoice.

docs.title: Dependencies & Requirements
docs.text: This page covers both operator (runtime) requirements for running TAK-XVoice on Android devices and developer (build) dependencies for compiling the plugin from source.

docs.title: Android & ATAK Versions
docs.text: Component Requirement Notes Android OS Android 8.0+ (API 26) Compiled and targeted against API 36 (targetSdk = 36, required by Google Play). ATAK CIV 5.6 / 5.7 / 5.8 The plugin's plugin-api manifest metadata must match your installed ATAK baseline. Play Store / TPP builds are published per supported baseline. TAK Server Enrolled in ATAK Device must have a valid TAK Server connection and TLS enrollment certificate configured in ATAK. Mumble Server Same hostname as TAK Server, port 64738 (TCP/UDP) Standard Mumble (Murmur) server reachable at your TAK Server's hostname with a valid TLS certificate. See Server & Channels.

docs.title: Android Permissions
docs.text:
TAK-XVoice requests only the permissions required for voice capture, Bluetooth routing, VoIP call management, and background reliability:

Permission Purpose RECORD_AUDIO, MODIFY_AUDIO_SETTINGS Microphone capture and audio routing during active PTT / calls. INTERNET, ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE Mumble TLS/UDP transport and observing Wi-Fi ↔ cellular handoffs. ACCESS_WIFI_STATE, CHANGE_WIFI_MULTICAST_STATE Acquiring Android's MulticastLock when alpha mesh-voice failover is enabled. BLUETOOTH_CONNECT, BLUETOOTH_SCAN (Android 12+) / BLUETOOTH, BLUETOOTH_ADMIN (Android ≤ 11) Discovering and connecting to Bluetooth speaker-mics and BLE PTT buttons (neverForLocation flag set — no location data accessed). MANAGE_OWN_CALLS, CALL_PHONE, READ_PHONE_STATE Android self-managed VoIP (ConnectionService) for clean audio focus arbitration and Bluetooth SCO routing. FOREGROUND_SERVICE (MICROPHONE, CONNECTED_DEVICE, PHONE_CALL) Keeping voice sessions and private calls alive when ATAK is backgrounded or the screen is off. POST_NOTIFICATIONS, USE_FULL_SCREEN_INTENT Foreground voice notification and full-screen incoming direct-call ring UI. REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS, WAKE_LOCK Preventing Android Doze from killing active voice sockets and handling earpiece proximity screen-off.

docs.title: Toolchain
docs.text:
• JDK 17 (jvmTarget = 17)
  • Gradle Wrapper (./gradlew / .\gradlew.bat, included in the repository)
  • Android SDK (compileSdk = 36, ndkVersion = 25.1.8937393 — pinned to match TAK TPP build hosts; XV has no JNI code)
  • ATAK CIV SDK (main.jar) — not bundled in this repository; obtain it separately from tak.gov under its own license terms.

docs.title: Core Runtime Libraries
docs.text: Library Role Kotlin stdlib & Coroutines (kotlinx-coroutines-android) Core language runtime and async audio/network pipelines. AndroidX (core-ktx, appcompat) Android platform compatibility helpers. Concentus (pure-Java Opus, via JitPack) Opus audio encoding/decoding without native NDK/JNI dependencies. Protobuf Java Lite (protobuf-javalite) Mumble wire protocol serialization with minimal APK overhead. ZXing Core (compileOnly) QR code encode/decode for offline comms-plan sharing (provided at runtime by ATAK; degrades gracefully to share sheet if absent).

docs.title: Building from Source
docs.text:
1. Place the matching ATAK CIV SDK main.jar into app/libs/main.jar (gitignored):
Copy-Item C:\path\to\ATAK-CIV-5.7.0-SDK\main.jar app\libs\main.jar
  1. Run tests, style checks, and build tasks:
.\gradlew test                 # Unit tests
.\gradlew ktlintCheck          # Kotlin style check
.\gradlew assembleCivDebug     # Debug APK (loads on Developer SDK ATAK)
.\gradlew assembleCivRelease   # Release APK (for TPP signing pipeline)
.\gradlew tppArchive           # Source zips for TPP upload (5.6 / 5.7 / 5.8)

Plugin Signing for Play Store ATAK

Play Store ATAK requires plugins to be signed through the TAK Third-Party Plugin (TPP) pipeline. For Google Play releases, upload the app-civ-release.aab returned by TPP unmodified so ATAK can validate the embedded TPP code-transparency signature. You can verify a bundle before publishing with scripts/verify-play-aab.ps1.

docs.title: Design decisions (enforced on this branch)
docs.text: Durable record of the load-bearing decisions behind channel sharing, multicast failover, and the audio plant, so future contributors don't re-litigate them. Each states the decision and the why, and cites the file that enforces it. If you think one of these is wrong, raise it with the operator before changing the behavior — several were paid for in field repros.

docs.title: 1. Recipient scoping rides on ATAK's contact model, not a plugin group
docs.text:
Channel share uses ATAK's native sharing model — individual / group / everyone — and delegates recipient scoping entirely to ATAK's own contact model. XV does not implement a plugin-side group to bound the blast radius.

Why: the TAK server's group membership is not reliably visible to a plugin locally, so any plugin-side "share only to my group" would be guessing at membership the plugin can't authoritatively see. Bounding the audience is the server's / ATAK's job; reimplementing it in the plugin is the wrong layer and would fork from what the operator sees in the ATAK contact list.

Enforced in: provisioning/XvChannelShare.kt (send() — empty targets → dispatchToBroadcast; specific targets → dispatchToContacts resolved through Contacts.fromUIDs).

docs.title: 2. Targeted shares fail closed — never fall back to broadcast
docs.text:
A directed share to specific recipients that cannot be resolved to live contacts returns false and sends nothing. It never degrades to a server broadcast.

Why: privacy. The wire targets attribute only filters who acts on a share, not who receives it. A targeted share that fell back to broadcast would disclose the channel name(s), the sharer's identity, and the server host to the entire server audience — the opposite of what the operator asked for. Failing closed and steering to the offline / QR path is the safe default.

Enforced in: provisioning/XvChannelShare.kt (send(), the contacts.isNullOrEmpty() guard) and ui/XvDropDownReceiver.kt (promptPickTeammatesThenShare → "Couldn't share over the network — use offline QR").

docs.title: 3. We do not share server connection info with third parties
docs.text:
A share — whether the CoT nudge or the offline comms plan — carries the channel configuration (and, offline, an optional pre-shared key) so a recipient can bring up multicast voice. It never carries the means to connect to and authenticate against the TAK / Mumble server (certs, credentials, a connection profile).

Why: a local-network third party may legitimately need to join the voice mesh, and the channel config plus key is exactly enough for that. It is not entitled to your server. The multicast config is self-sufficient for LAN voice — the receiver derives the endpoint (or uses a pinned group/port) without ever touching the server — so there is no reason to hand over server access to make voice work.

Enforced in: provisioning/CommsPlan.kt (the plan schema carries channels + optional psk + a derivation serverIdentity hint, and no server credentials) and plugin/XvMapComponent.kt (buildChannelPlanCarrierInternal).

docs.title: 4. Multicast group is deterministically derived, not exchanged
docs.text:
The failover multicast endpoint is a pure local hash: H = SHA-256("xv-mcast-v1|" + serverIdentity + "|" + canon(channelName)), mapped to group = 239.224.0.0/12 and port = 16800–16899.

Why: two peers on the same server and channel independently compute the byte-identical group + port with no broker and no coordination, so failover works the instant the Mumble server disappears — and the share signal only needs to carry the channel name, never the address or a key. Inputs are chosen for stability: the channel name (not the server-assigned numeric id, which changes when an admin rebuilds the tree) and the server hostname (not the cert fingerprint, which a renewal would silently fork mid-deployment). SHA-256 (not String.hashCode) keeps same-deployment collisions past observability.

Enforced in: transport/multicast/MulticastGroupDerivation.kt and transport/multicast/ServerIdentity.kt.

docs.title: 5. Mesh legs and MESH-source presence survive a Mumble server drop
docs.text:
Multicast failover legs and presence learned over the mesh are tracked independently of the TAK-server CoT path, and deliberately persist when the Mumble server drops.

Why: surviving a server outage is the entire point of the mesh. A channel's default multicast posture is FAILOVER — the RX leg is joined whenever the network is multicast-capable, which is how Mumble-down is survivable at all. MESH-source presence is kept in its own map so it does not vanish with the server-bound CoT roster; a peer heard only over multicast still shows as callable. Tearing either down on a server disconnect would blind the operator at exactly the moment failover is supposed to carry them.

Enforced in: transport/multicast/ChannelMulticastConfig.kt (MulticastMode.FAILOVER), presence/XvPresenceRegistry.kt (separate meshByUid map), and transport/multicast/MeshVoiceManager.kt (FailoverPolicy).

docs.title: 6. Phone stays a phone — no held audio resources between transmissions
docs.text:
XV holds no audio resources (no pre-armed mic session, no retained capture path) between PTT bursts. Readiness is established by probe/verify at TX time, not by keeping the plant warm.

Why: the device is still the operator's phone. Holding the mic or an audio route between transmissions starves other apps, drains battery, and fights the OS audio focus model. Probe-verified readiness is sanctioned; a persistently pre-armed session is not. HAL warmth is a property of recent activity, not of a per-record held resource.

Enforced in: service/VoicePlant.kt, audio/AudioCapture.kt, and audio/ScoLink.kt.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Get TAK-XVoice installed, connected to your TAK/Mumble server, and transmitting in a few minutes.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Make sure you have:

  • ATAK CIV installed and enrolled to your TAK Server (see Dependencies for supported baselines).
  • A Mumble (Murmur) server reachable at the same hostname as your TAK Server on the standard Mumble port 64738 (TCP/UDP). See Server & Channels for full server requirements.
  • (Optional) A supported Bluetooth speaker-mic or ruggedized handset from Supported Hardware.

docs.title: 1. Install TAK-XVoice
docs.text:
Google Play (Play Store ATAK)Developer / SDK Build
  1. Install TAK-XVoice from Google Play (or your managed Play / TPP distribution channel).
  2. Open ATAK.
  3. Go to Settings → Tool Preferences → Plugin Management (or tap the prompt when ATAK detects the newly installed plugin) and Load TAK-XVoice (XV).
  1. Build and install the debug APK against your matching ATAK CIV SDK baseline (see Dependencies → Building from Source).
  2. Launch ATAK CIV Developer Edition and load TAK-XVoice (XV) from Plugin Management.

docs.title: 2. Grant Required Permissions
docs.text:
When TAK-XVoice loads for the first time, grant the requested Android permissions:

  • Microphone (RECORD_AUDIO) — required to transmit voice.
  • Nearby Devices / Bluetooth (BLUETOOTH_CONNECT, BLUETOOTH_SCAN) — required to discover and route audio to Bluetooth speaker-mics and BLE PTT buttons.
  • Phone / Call Management (CALL_PHONE, READ_PHONE_STATE) — required by Android's self-managed VoIP Telecom framework for clean audio focus and Bluetooth routing.
  • Notifications (POST_NOTIFICATIONS) — required for the foreground voice service and incoming direct-call alerts.
  • Battery Optimization Exemption — recommended when prompted so Android Doze does not drop your voice socket while the screen is off.

docs.title: 3. Connect to Your Server & Join a Channel
docs.text:
1. Tap the TAK-XVoice (XV) walkie-talkie icon on the ATAK toolbar to open the XV drop-down panel.
  2. XV automatically discovers your configured TAK Server(s) from ATAK and connects to Mumble on that same hostname, port 64738, authenticating with your device's ATAK TLS enrollment certificate.
  3. If you have multiple TAK Servers configured in ATAK, open XV Settings to pick a preferred server host.
  4. Select a channel from the Mumble channel list to join.

No separate Mumble login needed

Because XV reuses your ATAK enrollment certificate for TLS client authentication, you do not need to enter a separate Mumble password. The server's TLS certificate must match the hostname you connect to.

docs.title: 4. Pair Your Speaker-Mic (Optional)
docs.text:
• AINA APTT V2 / V1 or Inrico BT02: Pair the speaker-mic in Android Bluetooth Settings first, then select it in XV Settings → Primary Speaker-Mic.
  • Pryme BT-PTT-Z (BLE button only): Follow the Pryme BT-PTT-Z Pairing Guide.
  • Samsung Active Key: Enable the hardware key toggle in XV Settings; see Samsung Active Key for background / screen-off setup.

docs.title: 5. Test Push-to-Talk
docs.text:
1. Press and hold the on-screen PTT button (or your paired speaker-mic / hardware PTT key).
  2. Listen for the Talk Permit Tone (if enabled) and speak.
  3. Release to stop transmitting.

Next: tune audio routing, auto-start missions, talk-permit tones, and emergency buttons in User Setup.

docs.title: Server & Channels
docs.text: TAK-XVoice uses Mumble (Murmur) for server-mediated voice alongside your existing TAK Server deployment. This page documents the current server layout requirements, TLS authentication model, and recommended channel management practices.

docs.title: Mumble Host & Port Requirements
docs.text:
Same Hostname & Standard Port Required

For the current release, the Mumble server must be hosted on the same host — or be accessible via the same hostname — as your TAK Server, and must listen on the standard Mumble port 64738 (TCP and UDP).

docs.title: Why this is required right now
docs.text:
TAK-XVoice automatically discovers your TAK Server(s) from ATAK's own connection list (TAKServerListener) and derives the Mumble endpoint directly from the TAK Server's hostname:

Parameter Value Notes Hostname Same hostname as your TAK Server Derived automatically from ATAK's configured TAK Server connection string (e.g., tak.example.com). Port 64738 (TCP + UDP) Standard Mumble port. TCP carries the TLS control channel (and fallback voice); UDP carries low-latency voice packets. Transport security TLS (mutual / client cert) Uses your device's ATAK enrollment certificate.

If your Mumble server runs on a separate backend machine or container, route traffic for <your-tak-hostname>:64738 (via reverse proxy, port forwarding, or shared ingress) so clients reach Mumble on the same hostname as the TAK Server.

docs.title: Multiple TAK Servers
docs.text:
If ATAK is configured with more than one TAK Server, XV picks a server in this order:

  1. Preferred host — if you explicitly selected a TAK Server in XV Settings, XV honors that exact hostname.
  2. First connected TAK Server — otherwise, XV picks the first currently connected server.
  3. First configured TAK Server — if ATAK is not actively connected to CoT, XV falls back to the first configured server so voice can still connect using the stored enrollment certificate.

docs.title: TLS Authentication & Hostname Verification
docs.text:
• Client certificate: XV authenticates to Mumble using the device's ATAK enrollment certificate (checking the server's specific certificate entry first, then falling back to ATAK's default client/trust certificates when a data package only populates the global entries).
  • Strict hostname verification: XV refuses to connect to a Mumble server whose TLS certificate does not match the hostname it is connecting to. Ensure the Mumble server presents a certificate whose SAN/CN covers the TAK Server hostname and chains to a CA trusted by ATAK.

docs.title: Channel Management & TAK Group Synchronization
docs.text: Voice channels are configured and managed by Mumble, not created or stored inside TAK-XVoice itself. Operators see and join the channel tree exposed by the Mumble server.

docs.title: Recommended: Synchronize Mumble Channels with TAK Server Groups
docs.text:
While you can manage Mumble channels manually, we recommend running an integration or synchronization interface that maps your TAK Server groups (or an existing organizational / identity group structure managed outside Mumble) into Mumble channels and ACLs.

Benefits of automated group-to-channel synchronization:

  • Single source of truth: Admins add or move operators in TAK Server (or their upstream directory/MDM) without manually mirroring changes in Murmur.
  • Consistent access control: Mumble channel ACLs stay aligned with TAK group membership so operators automatically see the voice channels for their assigned teams.
  • Faster event spin-up: Standing up a new event or mission group provisions the corresponding voice channel structure automatically.

(For example, OpenTAKServer and similar TAK stacks can host Murmur alongside the TAK Server on the same hostname and automate channel/group management.)

docs.title: Mission Auto-Channels (Opt-In)
docs.text:
TAK-XVoice also includes an opt-in Mission Auto-Channels toggle (off by default):

  • When enabled, the operator's active ATAK mission drives the primary voice channel — XV derives a deterministic channel name from the mission name, creates it on the Mumble server if it does not already exist (and the server permits channel creation), and joins it.
  • Manually switching to another channel hands control back to the operator until the active mission changes.
  • If the Mumble server denies channel creation, XV notifies the operator rather than failing silently.

docs.title: User Setup & Configuration
docs.text: Once TAK-XVoice is installed and connected (see Quick Start), use this guide to configure audio routing, Bluetooth hardware, background PTT, tones, emergency alerts, and channel sharing.

docs.title: Audio Routing ("Phone Stays a Phone")
docs.text:
TAK-XVoice treats your paired Bluetooth speaker-mic as XV-exclusive comms gear while leaving the rest of your phone alone:

  • No held audio resources: HFP/SCO is engaged only while the mic is actively open (PTT-down or hot-mic). Loading the plugin or joining a channel does not hijack your audio route.
  • Media & navigation keep working: Spotify, podcasts, GPS turn-by-turn prompts, ATAK alerts, and personal headphones continue using their normal A2DP / phone audio paths between transmissions.

docs.title: Bluetooth Speaker-Mic Picker & Fallback
docs.text:
Open XV Settings → Primary Speaker-Mic to pick your preferred Bluetooth device:

  • Reachability-aware picker: On plugin load, XV restores your last-connected speaker-mic if it is reachable; otherwise it automatically selects the first live supported device. Unreachable pairings are dimmed and non-tappable in the picker so you can see at a glance what is powered on.
  • Automatic fallback & recovery: If your selected Bluetooth device becomes unreachable for 15 seconds during a session, XV falls back to the phone speaker while remembering your preferred MAC address — audio automatically returns to the speaker-mic as soon as it reconnects.
  • Per-MAC button defaults & overrides: Each supported device ships pre-mapped (PTT → Channel 1, secondary → Channel 2, emergency button, prev/next channel) so a fresh pairing works out of the box. Any custom button overrides you make persist per Bluetooth MAC address.

For device-specific pairing and button notes, see Supported Hardware.

docs.title: Background & Screen-Off Hardware PTT
docs.text:
The Samsung Active Key works as PTT in the foreground, with ATAK backgrounded, and with the screen locked once it is assigned to XV in Samsung's own settings:

  1. Open XV Settings and tap Samsung Active Key PTT (visible only on devices with the key). XV opens Samsung's Active button settings screen.
  2. Turn on Use Active button with app and pick Texas TAK-XVoice.
  3. Back in XV Settings the row shows Assigned.

No special permissions

This uses Samsung's built-in key mapping. XV needs no accessibility service, Knox license or extra permission for it. Turn the Samsung setting off to give the key back to Samsung.

docs.title: Auto-Start & Startup Mission
docs.text:
• Remember last mission: By default, XV remembers your last-used mission and automatically reconnects when ATAK starts — no need to re-open the plugin and re-join after every restart.
  • Fleet startup mission: For managed deployments, you can configure a fixed startup mission in XV Settings so every device lands on the right voice channel on boot.

docs.title: Talk Permit Tones
docs.text:
For operators transitioning from public-safety LMR radios, XV provides configurable Talk Permit Tones in XV Settings:

  • ASTRO 25
  • Nextel
  • DMR
  • MOTOTRBO
  • None

docs.title: LMR-Style Emergency Button
docs.text:
Supported speaker-mics include an LMR-style emergency workflow wired directly into ATAK's Alert Tool:

  • Short press: Fires the emergency beacon configured in ATAK's Alert Tool.
  • Long press (1 second): Cancels / disarms an active emergency.

Inrico BT02 Exception

On the experimental Inrico BT02, a 2-second hold on SOS only fires the emergency — it cannot disarm it. You must cancel an active emergency from ATAK's Emergency / Alert tool. See Inrico BT02.

docs.title: Direct Calling
docs.text:
You can place private, 1-to-1 calls to peers on your server or mesh presence roster:

  • Uses Android's Notification.CallStyle ring and a full-screen incoming-call surface.
  • Holds a proximity wake-lock when using the earpiece route so the screen turns off when held to your ear.

docs.title: Channel Sharing & Offline Comms Plans
docs.text:
Share channels with teammates in two ways:

  • Over the TAK Server (CoT nudge): Share to Everyone (broadcast) or to specific teammates using ATAK's native contact list. Targeted shares fail closed — if recipients cannot be resolved to live contacts, nothing is broadcast and XV steers you to the offline QR flow instead.
  • Offline QR / Comms Plan: Export a channel configuration (and optional passphrase-locked pre-shared key for encrypted mesh channels) as a QR code or shareable plan. Comms plans never include TAK/Mumble server credentials or certificates.

docs.title: Mesh-Voice Failover (Alpha — Testing Only)
docs.text:
Alpha Feature — Off by Default

Mesh-voice failover is experimental and for testing only. It is off by default and has a known bridge issue on congested networks under investigation. Do not rely on it operationally until it graduates.

When enabled in XV Settings:

  • Every joined channel automatically gets a deterministically derived LAN multicast leg (xv-mcast-v1, mapped to 239.224.0.0/12, ports 16800–16899) computed from the server hostname and channel name — no address exchange required.
  • Voice fails over to multicast when the Mumble server is unreachable and fails back automatically when the server returns.
  • Supports per-frame AEAD encryption (ChaCha20-Poly1305) with TAK-cert-wrapped channel keys, distributed key election, auto-bridge election, and pinned group/port overrides for OpenMANET / mesh-radio interop (standard RTP RFC 3550 + 7587 or raw-Opus wire mode).

docs.title: Field-verification checklist — channel share
docs.text:
Operator-runnable smoke test for the CoT channel-share feature (the passphrase/string-free "join my channel" nudge). It verifies the current behavior on this branch: sharing to Everyone broadcasts to your server contacts; sharing to specific teammates is a directed send that fails closed (nothing goes out, no broadcast) if the recipients can't be resolved, and the UI then steers you to the offline / QR path.

Run it with two XV devices before shipping a build that touches sharing, presence, or multicast derivation. Tick each box.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• [ ] Two XV devices (call them Alpha and Bravo), both on ATAK-CIV Developer edition, both enrolled to the same TAK server (tak.example.com) and showing each other in the Recent Users / presence roster.
  • [ ] Mesh voice is enabled on both, on the same L2 network (multicast-capable Wi-Fi), so a derived failover leg can actually come up.
  • [ ] At least one channel exists on Alpha to share (an encrypted one is the more interesting case).

docs.title: Everyone-share (broadcast)
docs.text:
• [ ] On Alpha, open the share flow, pick one or more channels, choose Everyone, and Send. Alpha toasts Shared N channel(s).
  • [ ] Bravo raises a "Join shared channel(s)?" prompt naming the sharer, the channel(s), and (if known) the server. Tap Join.
  • [ ] Both devices independently derive the same multicast group:port for that channel name — they converge without the address ever being on the wire (derivation is (serverIdentity, channelName) → 239.224.0.0/12 : 16800–16899). Confirm mesh voice passes both directions.
  • [ ] For an encrypted channel, the key auto-exchanges over the existing election — no passphrase was typed and no key was on the share wire. Encrypted mesh audio decodes on both ends.
  • [ ] Send the same Everyone-share again. Bravo does not re-prompt for the duplicate delivery (dedup by share event UID; server backlog replay and multi-path copies must not re-pop Join).

docs.title: Individual-target share (directed)
docs.text:
• [ ] With a third device (or by targeting only Bravo), share to a specific teammate. Only the addressee prompts; other presence-roster peers do not see a Join prompt.
  • [ ] Confirm the addressee joins and hears mesh voice as above.

docs.title: Targeted share with an unresolvable / stale contact (fail-closed)
docs.text:
This is the privacy-critical case. A targeted share must never fall back to a server-wide broadcast.

  • [ ] Target a teammate whose contact is stale/unresolvable (e.g. the peer just dropped off the server, or pick a roster entry that no longer resolves to a live contact) and Send.
  • [ ] Nothing is dispatched. No third party — and specifically not the whole-server audience — receives a Join prompt or sees the channel name / sharer / server host. (The wire targets attribute only filters who acts; it does not limit who receives, which is exactly why a targeted share is never broadcast.)
  • [ ] Alpha shows the toast "Couldn't share over the network — use offline QR." and the offline share path opens automatically.
  • [ ] Nothing leaked to the server: confirm no other roster device prompted.

docs.title: Offline comms-plan import/export regression
docs.text:
• [ ] From the offline path (the fallback above, or the explicit Offline / QR button), export a comms plan for a keyless channel. It encodes clear — no passphrase demanded.
  • [ ] Export a plan for a channel that carries a key. It is passphrase-locked; a blank passphrase is refused.
  • [ ] Import each plan on the other device. A keyless plan imports and the channel becomes visible + joinable in the picker; a locked plan imports only with the correct passphrase.
  • [ ] Import round-trips: an accepted plan's channels persist across an ATAK restart (force-stop com.atakmap.app.civ, relaunch) and are still in the picker — not just the auto-primary.

docs.title: What to capture (and what NOT to commit)
docs.text:
• Watch these log tags: XvChannelShare (send / parse / fail-closed decisions), XvCotListener (inbound share + presence), and XV (accept / join / derivation).
  • The fail-closed line to look for on a blocked targeted share: send: targeted recipients unresolved — failing closed (no broadcast).
  • Do NOT commit raw field logs. logcat / dumpsys captures routinely contain Bluetooth MACs, device serials, real TAK hostnames, and call metadata. Keep captures under logs/ / diagnostics/ (already gitignored) and never git add -f them. If you need to quote a line in an issue or PR, scrub hostnames to tak.example, MACs to XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX, and callsigns to Alpha / Bravo first.

docs.title: Hardware setup guides
docs.text:
Device-specific setup and behavior notes for the ruggedized handsets and speakermics TAK-XVoice supports. These pages cover the parts that vary by chassis — which physical keys map to what, the OS settings an operator has to touch, and the foreground vs. background behavior.

For the curated-hardware policy (what "supported" means and why a device is or isn't listed), see Hardware Philosophy.

docs.title: On-device hardware keys
docs.text: • Samsung Active Key — programmable side key on Galaxy Tab Active5 / Active4 Pro / Active3 and XCover6 Pro / 7.

docs.title: Bluetooth speakermics
docs.text:
The curated / validated Bluetooth speakermics (AINA APTT V2 — #1 recommended, AINA APTT V1 — #2 recommended, and Pryme BT-PTT-Z external button) are registered per-MAC and mapped to channels automatically; see the top-level README's "What's different" and "Hardware tested" sections.

  • Pryme BT-PTT-Z Pairing Guide — instructions and troubleshooting for Pryme BLE PTT buttons.
  • Inrico BT02 (B02) — budget / experimental speaker-mic with limited support (available for testing, subject to removal).

docs.title: Retired hardware
docs.text:
Devices that were supported at one point and have since been dropped. The pages are kept so existing links resolve to an explanation of what changed and why, rather than a 404.

  • Sonim XP10 (XP9900) — retired. Dropped for device stability and Bluetooth reliability problems that made it unsuitable as a custom-button integration target, compounded by an end-of-life platform with no further security updates.

docs.title: Inrico BT02 (B02) — Budget / Experimental Speaker-Mic
docs.text: Status: Experimental / Limited Support — Subject to Removal. The Inrico BT02 (also sold as the Inrico B02) is included as a budget option for testing because of community interest in supporting lower-cost Bluetooth speaker-mics. It is not a recommended replacement for AINA hardware, receives limited support, and may be removed in a future release if it proves unreliable in field traffic. For production use, choose the AINA PTT Voice Responder V2 (#1 recommended) or AINA PTT Voice Responder V1 (#2 recommended).

docs.title: Why it's included (and what "budget option" means)
docs.text:
Operators frequently ask whether XVoice can work with inexpensive Zello-style Bluetooth speaker-mics. The Inrico BT02 meets the minimum criteria for basic testing (Classic HFP speaker/mic audio, physical PTT, and a dedicated SOS button), so it is supported experimentally as a budget tier.

With a budget device come budget capabilities and hardware limitations:

  • Lower microphone gain and audio fidelity compared to AINA V1/V2 speakermics. XVoice applies a +5 dB (1.78x) software mic-gain boost automatically when capturing over BT02 Bluetooth SCO, but acoustic clarity and wind/noise rejection remain below AINA hardware.
  • Emergency (SOS) button ONLY triggers — it CANNOT disable/disarm an emergency: The BT02 firmware requires a 2-second press-and-hold before transmitting its emergency event (0x08) and never sends a release event. Because of this hardware limitation, holding SOS for 2 seconds only fires ATAK's emergency beacon — it does not cancel or turn it off. If you trigger an emergency with this budget speaker-mic, you MUST disable/disarm it from the ATAK app (Emergency / Alert tool). By contrast, on AINA PTT Voice Responders (V1 and V2), a 1-second long press on the speaker-mic disables / turns off an active emergency directly.
  • Top / group switch button is unmapped. Only the primary PTT and SOS buttons are mapped.
  • No secondary channel (VS2) button.

docs.title: Pairing (one-step Classic Bluetooth)
docs.text:
Pair the BT02 in Android Bluetooth Settings just like an AINA speaker-mic — do not use XV's "Scan for BLE PTT device" button:

  1. Power the Inrico BT02 completely off.
  2. Press and hold the Power button (~5–6 seconds) until the LED flashes red and blue alternating (Classic pairing mode).
  3. Open Android Settings → Connected devices → Pair new device and pair the B02PTT-xxxx Classic Bluetooth audio entry (with Headset / Call audio).
  4. Note: The BT02 also advertises an unbonded BLE peripheral with the same B02PTT-xxxx name. If Android hangs while pairing, make sure the LED is flashing red/blue (Classic pairing mode) and you are pairing the Classic audio entry rather than the BLE-only advertisement.
  5. Open ATAK / XVoice. B02PTT-xxxx appears in the Primary Speaker-Mic picker just like an AINA. When selected (or auto-connected), XVoice routes HFP audio to the Classic device and automatically discovers and connects to the companion BLE button link in the background.

docs.title: Button mapping
docs.text: Physical button Action Notes PTT (side) Transmit on primary channel Press and hold to talk; release to stop. SOS / Emergency Fire ATAK emergency beacon Press and hold 2 seconds to fire. Fire-only — cancel active emergency in ATAK's Emergency tool. Top / group button Unmapped Intentionally ignored. Volume +/- Local speaker volume Handled on the speaker-mic hardware.

docs.title: Important Pairing Instructions
docs.text:
DO NOT pair Pryme BT-PTT-Z buttons via the main Android OS Bluetooth settings.

Many dual-mode BLE PTT pucks (such as the Pryme BT-PTT-Z and other inexpensive clones) have a known hardware defect where they drop their Bluetooth bonding keys whenever they are powered off.

If you pair the device in the Android Bluetooth settings: 1. Android saves a "Long Term Key" (LTK) for the device. 2. When the device is turned off and back on, it forgets the key. 3. When Android connects to it again, Android attempts to re-establish the encrypted connection. The PTT puck rejects it ("PIN or Key Missing"). 4. Android aggressively deletes the bond entirely and throws an annoying "Pairing Request" prompt to the user. 5. This cycle will repeat every time you turn the puck on and off, or every time you press the button (if it tries to wake up its HID keyboard profile).

docs.title: Correct Setup
docs.text:
1. If you have already paired the Bluetooth button in Android, go to your Android Settings > Connected Devices / Bluetooth, find the Bluetooth device, and select Forget or Unpair.
  2. Put the Pryme puck in pairing mode.
  3. Open the TAK-XVoice plugin.
  4. Go to the plugin's Bluetooth device picker.
  5. Select and connect to the Pryme device directly from the app.

By avoiding standard OS-level bonding, the app connects to the button via an unencrypted GATT data channel. This channel survives app restarts and power cycles perfectly without ever triggering Android's pairing prompt loops.

docs.title: Note on Generic Media Buttons
docs.text: If you are using a generic Bluetooth media/volume remote (such as inexpensive Amazon camera shutter / media buttons) rather than a dedicated PTT puck, those should be paired in the standard Android OS settings. They typically have stable bonding firmware and act strictly as HID input devices, which the ATAK plugin supports natively by intercepting the Volume/Media keystrokes.

docs.title: Samsung Active Key (ruggedized tablets & phones)
docs.text: Samsung ruggedized hardware ships with a programmable Active Key — a physical side button — that TAK-XVoice can use as a Push-To-Talk source alongside (or instead of) a Bluetooth speakermic.

docs.title: Supported chassis
docs.text:
The Samsung Active Key PTT settings row appears only on hardware that actually has the key. XV recognizes:

Family Build.MODEL prefix Galaxy Tab Active5 SM-X300 / SM-X306 / SM-X308 Galaxy Tab Active4 Pro SM-T630 / SM-T636 Galaxy Tab Active3 SM-T570 / SM-T575 / SM-T577 Galaxy XCover7 SM-G556 Galaxy XCover6 Pro SM-G736

On any other device the row is hidden and this feature is a no-op.

docs.title: The two keys
docs.text:
• Active Key (side) — keyCode 1015. This is the PTT source.
  • Top / Emergency key — keyCode 1079. Not wired to PTT or the emergency alert today; it keeps its Samsung-configured behavior.

docs.title: Setup — assign the key to XV
docs.text:
Samsung's own setting is the single on/off switch. Once the key is assigned to XV it works as PTT in the foreground, with ATAK backgrounded, and with the screen off and locked. This uses Samsung's built-in "control the key with an app" mapping. It needs no accessibility service, no Knox SDK and no Knox license.

  1. In XV settings, tap Samsung Active Key PTT. XV opens Samsung's Active button screen. (You can also go there yourself: Settings → Advanced features → Active button.)
  2. Turn on Use Active button with app and pick Texas TAK-XVoice.
  3. Press and hold the key — XV now receives every press and release, whatever is in the foreground.

XV has no toggle of its own. The row shows Assigned when Samsung's setting points at XV and Set up otherwise. Turn the Samsung setting off to give the key back to Samsung.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Samsung addresses a HARD_KEY_REPORT broadcast (keyCode 1015, report type 1 = press, 2 = release) to only the app the operator assigned the key to. XV is offered in that picker because its manifest declares:

  • a <meta-data> entry com.samsung.android.knox.intent.action.HARD_KEY_PRESS set to true, and
  • an exported receiver (SamsungHardKeyReceiver) for the com.samsung.android.knox.intent.action.HARD_KEY_REPORT action.

Without both, the app never appears in Samsung's picker and receives nothing.

Samsung's "Use while screen locked" toggle is a separate setting for using the key to open an app over the lock screen. It was off during validation and PTT still worked with the screen locked.

docs.title: On-device validation
docs.text:
• Galaxy Tab Active5 (SM-X308U, Android 16) — validated end to end: Active Key PTT transmits in the foreground, with ATAK backgrounded, and with the screen off and locked, with the key assigned to XV and no accessibility service installed.

Other listed chassis are gated on by model prefix but have not yet been validated end-to-end — see the curated-hardware policy in the top-level README.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Row missing: the device model isn't in the supported list above, or Build.MANUFACTURER isn't samsung.
  • Key does nothing in XV: the key isn't assigned to XV (the XV row shows Set up). Tap the row and confirm Use Active button with app is on and set to XV.
  • XV isn't offered in Samsung's picker: the firmware may not offer this mapping to third-party apps, or an older XV build without the manifest entries is installed.
  • Nothing happens at all: confirm Samsung's Active button isn't set to a "launch app" press or press-and-hold action, which swallows the key press.
  • Seeing whether reports arrive: each report XV receives is logged under the tag XvSamsungHardKeyRx (adb logcat -s XvSamsungHardKeyRx). Reports are dropped, with a log line, when no voice session is running.

docs.title: Sonim XP10 (XP9900) — support retired
docs.text:
Status: retired. TAK-XVoice no longer supports the Sonim XP10 / XP9900. The device-specific readers, the Build.BRAND / Build.MODEL gate, the settings row, and the AIDL surface that backed them were removed. This page is kept as a pointer so existing links resolve to an explanation rather than a 404.

If you are looking for a supported ruggedized handset with on-device hardware keys, see Samsung Active Key.

docs.title: Why support was removed
docs.text:
The XP10 was integrated and carried as a supported device for a period, then retired. The decision was driven by device behavior observed during integration and field testing, not by a change in what XV needs from a handset:

  • It did not meet the project's stability bar. The handset showed persistent instability across testing on a clean OS install — not traceable to XV's own state machines, and not resolved by reflashing or by carrier firmware updates.
  • It was problematic under performance and endurance testing. Behavior was inconsistent run-to-run, which made it unusable as a reference device: a failure on the XP10 could not be trusted to indicate an XV regression, and a pass could not be trusted to indicate a fix.
  • Bluetooth was the disqualifying problem. The handset had serious, reproducible Bluetooth issues. Because XV's speakermic and BLE-button integration depends on a dependable Bluetooth stack — SCO setup and teardown, bonded-device reconnect, and HID/SPP button event delivery — a handset whose Bluetooth cannot be relied on is a poor candidate for custom button integration. This is the reason the device was dropped rather than kept on a best-effort basis.
  • End-of-life with no security update path. The platform is approaching vendor end-of-life without further security patches. Carrying a supported device that will not receive updates is inconsistent with the project's security posture.

Taken together, the maintenance cost of four device-specific readers and a bespoke AIDL surface was not justified by a device that could not be trusted as a test target and could not be recommended to operators.

docs.title: What this means in practice
docs.text:
• XV will install and run on an XP10 — nothing blocks it — but the dedicated PTT key, the SOS / Emergency key, and the Programmable-Keys "assign to ATAK" mode are no longer wired to XV.
  • On-screen PTT and Bluetooth speakermic PTT behave as they do on any other handset, subject to the Bluetooth caveats above.
  • No migration is required for other hardware. The Samsung Active Key path is unaffected.
